Anonymous authors

Paper under double-blind review

# ABSTRACT

In professional video editing, an agent's output is not a rendered video but an editable project that human editors continue to work on. Thus, rigorous evaluation of video-editing agents requires both scalable construction of realistic editing tasks and systematic verification of such project states. We introduce [NAME C05], a benchmark of 781 video-editing tasks that connects task construction and outcome evaluation through a shared structured specification. [NAME C05] extracts real workflows from official editing tutorials and organizes them into 48 atomic editing operations and 121 reusable task templates. Each atomic operation specifies both the edit to perform and evaluation rules for the requested changes and required preservation, allowing natural-language instructions and their evaluation to come from the same task specification. [NAME C05] evaluates agents directly on the resulting project state,

### 3.3 CONTROLLABLE EXECUTION ENVIRONMENT

We use two environments to run [NAME C05]: (1) [NAME C05] as the primary execution environment for large-scale parallel experiments and (2) Adobe Premiere Pro as the target environment for verifying application fidelity in realistic professional video editing.

[NAME C05]. [NAME C05] requires a scalable, web-based video-editing environment for parallel agent testing. We implemented [NAME C05], our benchmark environment built as an instrumented fork of the MIT-licensed OpenCut Classic editor (OpenCut Project). When an episode ends, it automatically exports the current project state in JSON format. Out of the 48 operations defined in [NAME C05], 19 were newly implemented in [NAME C05], while 29 were already provided th

### 4.1 TUTORIAL-BASED TASK TEMPLATE CONSTRUCTION

We use task templates as the foundation for generating multiple instances. A task template abstracts a single editing request as the required sequence of operations. A concrete task instance is created after binding the video, target clip, and parameter values.

Task template construction proceeds by (1) extracting source workflows from official editing tutorials, (2) organizing these workflows into common atomic operations, and (3) composing the operations into a task template.

Source Workflow Extraction. A workflow is an ordered sequence of editing operations, together with their target relationships, that fulfills a coherent editing request. For example, duplicating a clip and applying an effect to its copy forms a single workflow: creating a modified copy while preserving the original. We collected 45 official tutorial documents for three representative video-editing applications, Adobe Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro, and DaVinci Resolve, and extracted 165 source workflows from them.

Object Identification. An object is an individually identifiable editable element. Video clips, audio clips, and text graphics are representative objects, while timing, effects, and parameters are expressed as attributes of these objects. We match objects across $S_0$ and $S_T$ by their object IDs in [NAME C05]. Since IDs are not reliably preserved in XML exports, we additionally use track, media-reference, and timing information in Premiere Pro. Split, duplicate, and insert operations create objects that exist only in $S_T$. For such targets, the evaluator identifies the new object produced by the corresponding operation, using its source media and expected interval, and then evaluates the predicates on that object.

### 6.2 MAIN RESULTS

GPT-6 Sol achieves the highest success rate at 87.20%, followed by GPT-5.6 Sol at 84.25% (Table 1). Both Luna models outperform GPT-5.4 mini, while the two open-weight agents complete fewer than 5% of tasks. OpenCUA has higher request coverage but lower success than UI-TARS, showing that partial completion does not necessarily yield task success. Preservation coverage is high for proprietary models (96.94–99.82%) but lower for UI-TARS (85.70%) and OpenCUA (85.50%).

In this work, we used generative AI tools for assisting with the generation of a synthetic benchmark dataset, providing feedback on the research methodology and experimental design, implementing methods, translation, cleaning and reformatting dataset, and interpreting results. We have not used generative AI tools for developing the conceptual framework, and formulating mathematical claims, providing critical ingredients for proving mathematical claims, developing or writing proofs, proposing or refining hypotheses, and qualitative or thematic data analysis are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to create and edit software code, search for and summarize relevant literature, prepare scientific figures and research artifacts, and revise the manuscript. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. ABSTRACT
While In-Context Learning (ICL) enables models to adapt from exemplars without
parameter updates, multimodal ICL remains largely underexplored, particularly
regarding video demonstrations in interactive environments. For multimodal agents,
learning from videos presents unique challenges: they must translate in-context
demonstrations into executable policies, ground these policies in novel visual states,
and iteratively refine actions based on environmental feedback. We introduce V-
ICAL, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate video-based ICL for multimodal
agents. Comprising 342 interactive tasks across 37 environments, V-ICAL utilizes
human-curated demonstration videos as task-specific behavioral exemplars, evaluat-
ing agents through sustained interaction from a target initialization. The benchmark
seamlessly connects in-context knowledge induction wit
